books.title: The King and Queen of Sparta
A Day for Songs and Contests
The Prince Sets Sail for Home

herald.text: Book 1. Athena Inspires the Prince. A king named Odysseus left his island of Ithaca to fight a ten-year war at Troy, and ten more years have passed without his return. At home his wife and son wait while a crowd of local men eat his food and press his wife to marry one of them and take his throne. Now the gods decide to bring him home. Scene 1. The Gods Consider Odysseus. The gods meet, and Athena asks Zeus to let Odysseus go home, while the sea god who hates him is away.

greek.greek: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε·
greek.english: Father Zeus, let Aegisthus lie in the ruin he earned.

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Scene 2. Athena's Two-Part Plan. Athena plans to free Odysseus from the island where a goddess holds him, and to go herself to wake up his son.

greek.greek: οὐ γάρ πω τέθνηκεν ἐπὶ χθονὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
greek.english: hard-enduring Odysseus goes home.

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 3. The Stranger at the Threshold. Disguised as a traveling stranger, Athena arrives at Odysseus's house, where the suitors are feasting, and Telemachus welcomes her in.

greek.greek: ἔγχος μέν ῥʼ ἔστησε φέρων πρὸς κίονα μακρὴν
greek.english: give me your spear.

theme.means: grey-eyed, bright-eyed: Athena's epithet

herald.text: Scene 4. Mentes Questions the Prince. Telemachus complains that the suitors are eating up his missing father's wealth; the disguised goddess tells him his father is alive.

greek.greek: νῦν δʼ ὧδε ξὺν νηὶ κατήλυθον ἠδʼ ἑτάροισιν
greek.english: I am Mentes, son of wise Anchialus, lord of the oar-loving Taphians, and your father's guest-friend of old;

theme.means: the open sea

herald.text: Scene 5. Athena Arms Telemachus with a Course. Athena tells Telemachus to stand up to the suitors in public and to sail away in search of news of his father.

greek.greek: νῆʼ ἄρσας ἐρέτῃσιν ἐείκοσιν, ἥ τις ἀρίστη,
greek.english: Then fit out a ship of twenty oars and go for news of your long-gone father, to Nestor at Pylos first,

theme.means: the singer, the bard: the poem's own maker inside the poem

herald.text: Scene 6. The Goddess Departs; the Prince Speaks. The goddess flies off like a bird; Telemachus, newly bold, sends his grieving mother upstairs and calls a public meeting for dawn.

greek.greek: ἐκ τοῦ δʼ οὔτʼ Ὀδυσῆα ἐγὼν ἴδον οὔτʼ ἔμʼ ἐκεῖνος.
greek.english: Odysseus is not the only man who never came home from Troy.

theme.means: glory, what is heard of a man: fame that outlives him in song

herald.text: Book 2. Telemachus Sets Sail. At dawn Telemachus calls the people of Ithaca together for the first time in twenty years and demands that the suitors leave his house. The suitors refuse and blame his mother. With Athena's help, he prepares to slip away by ship to find news of his father. Scene 1. Telemachus Calls the Assembly. Telemachus summons the island to a meeting, sits in his father's seat, and stands to speak about the ruin of his house.

greek.greek: νῦν δʼ αὖ καὶ πολὺ μεῖζον, ὃ δὴ τάχα οἶκον ἅπαντα
greek.english: and now a greater ruin besides, suitors who beset my mother against her will and devour my house day after day.

theme.means: a trick, a snare: the horse, the bed, the web Penelope weaves and unweaves

herald.text: Scene 2. The Secret of Penelope's Loom. Antinous blames Penelope, who stalled the suitors for years by weaving a burial cloth by day and secretly unpicking it at night.

greek.greek: νύκτας δʼ ἀλλύεσκεν, ἐπεὶ δαΐδας παραθεῖτο.
greek.english: All day she wove at that web, and every night, with torches set beside her, she unraveled it thread by thread.

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Scene 3. The Eagles Tear the Air. Two eagles fight above the crowd; an old seer says Odysseus is coming home to punish the suitors, and Eurymachus mocks him.

greek.greek: ὤλετο τῆλʼ, ὡς καὶ σὺ καταφθίσθαι σὺν ἐκείνῳ
greek.english: Odysseus is dead far away, and a pity you did not die with him.

theme.means: the homecoming. The Odyssey is the poem of one man's nostos; our word nostalgia is the ache for it

herald.text: Scene 4. Mentor Rebukes Ithaca. Telemachus announces a voyage for news; Mentor scolds the people for doing nothing, but the suitors break up the meeting.

greek.greek: ἐξελάσαι μεγάροιο μενοινήσειʼ ἐνὶ θυμῷ,
greek.english: if Ithacan Odysseus himself came home and found us feasting in his hall and set his heart on driving us out,

theme.means: cunning intelligence, the craft of the mind. Odysseus's own gift, and Athena's

herald.text: Scene 5. Athena Answers on the Shore. Alone on the beach, Telemachus prays; Athena appears in Mentor's shape and promises to find him a ship and crew.

greek.greek: ὅς τοι νῆα θοὴν στελέω καὶ ἅμʼ ἕψομαι αὐτός.
greek.english: I sailed with your father of old, and I will sail with you, and find you a swift ship besides.

theme.means: an oath, sworn on the gods

herald.text: Scene 6. The Secret Stores. Telemachus secretly orders supplies from the storeroom, and his old nurse Eurycleia, frightened, swears not to tell his mother.

greek.greek: σοὶ δʼ ὁδὸς οὐκέτι δηρὸν ἀπέσσεται ἣν σὺ μενοινᾷς·
greek.english: You are an only son, beloved, and the sea will eat you as it ate him;

theme.means: a fool, a child: the one who does not see what is coming

herald.text: Scene 7. The Night Launch. Athena gathers a crew, puts the suitors to sleep, and sails with Telemachus through the night.

greek.greek: σοὶ δʼ ὁδὸς οὐκέτι δηρὸν ἀπέσσεται ἣν σὺ μενοινᾷς·
greek.english: Your companions sit at the oars already, waiting on your word;

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Book 3. King Nestor Remembers. Telemachus lands at Pylos, kingdom of an old king who fought beside his father at Troy. He hopes to learn what happened to Odysseus after the war. Athena travels with him, still disguised as his father's old friend Mentor. Scene 1. Arrival at Poseidon's Sacrifice. They arrive during a great sacrifice to the sea god; shy Telemachus is urged forward; Nestor's son welcomes them to the feast.

greek.greek: Τηλέμαχʼ, ἄλλα μὲν αὐτὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶ σῇσι νοήσεις,
greek.english: Telemachus, no more shyness, not now;

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 2. Telemachus Questions Nestor. Nestor asks who the strangers are; Telemachus names himself and begs for the plain truth about his father.

greek.greek: ἡμεῖς ἐξ Ἰθάκης ὑπονηίου εἰλήλουθμεν·
greek.english: Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans, we come from Ithaca below Neion, and the errand is my own:

theme.means: shame, reverence: the sense that stops a man from doing wrong before others and the gods

herald.text: Scene 3. The Broken Return from Troy. Nestor remembers how the Greek fleet split after the war; Odysseus went another way, and Nestor never learned what became of him.

greek.greek: καὶ σὺ φίλος, μάλα γάρ σʼ ὁρόω καλόν τε μέγαν τε,
greek.english: They say the Myrmidons came safe, and Philoctetes, and Idomeneus lost not a man the war had spared;

theme.means: the wife, she who shares the bed

herald.text: Scene 4. Orestes as the Measure. Nestor tells how Agamemnon was murdered at home and his son Orestes avenged him, and urges Telemachus to be just as brave.

greek.greek: τῷ δέ οἱ ὀγδοάτῳ κακὸν ἤλυθε δῖος Ὀρέστης
greek.english: in the eighth year Orestes returned from Athens and killed his father's murderer,

theme.means: rosy-fingered: the dawn's epithet, the formula that opens a new day

herald.text: Scene 5. Athena Reveals Herself at Pylos. The disguised companion suddenly flies off as a bird; Nestor realizes a goddess has been guiding Telemachus and prays to her.

greek.greek: οἱ δʼ ἄλλοι μένετʼ αὐτοῦ ἀολλέες, εἴπατε δʼ εἴσω
greek.english: grant fair fame to me, to my children, to my honored wife, and I will sacrifice to you a yearling heifer,

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 6. The Chariot Road to Sparta. Nestor gives Telemachus horses and a chariot, and his son Pisistratus drives him overland toward Sparta.

greek.greek: ἂν δʼ ἄρα Τηλέμαχος περικαλλέα βήσετο δίφρον·
greek.english: Quickly now, my sons, harness the flowing-maned horses to the car for Telemachus,

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Book 4. The King and Queen of Sparta. Telemachus reaches Sparta, ruled by Menelaus and his wife Helen, who both knew his father at Troy. They tell him stories of Odysseus and, at last, real news. Meanwhile, back on Ithaca, the suitors discover he has left. Scene 1. The Double Wedding at Sparta. Telemachus and Pisistratus arrive at Sparta during a wedding feast, and King Menelaus welcomes them into his dazzling palace.

greek.greek: Ζηνός που τοιήδε γʼ Ὀλυμπίου ἔνδοθεν αὐλή,
greek.english: Surely the court of Zeus on Olympus is like this;

theme.means: the singer, the bard: the poem's own maker inside the poem

herald.text: Scene 2. Recognition through Tears. When Menelaus speaks of Odysseus, Telemachus hides his tears; Helen recognizes him as Odysseus's son by his face, and all weep.

greek.greek: τὴν δʼ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
greek.english: Menelaus, shall I speak what my eyes tell me?

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 3. Helen's Drug and the Beggar in Troy. Helen eases their grief with a drugged wine and recalls Odysseus sneaking into the enemy city disguised as a beggar.

greek.greek: τῷ ἴκελος κατέδυ Τρώων πόλιν, οἱ δʼ ἀβάκησαν
greek.english: into the city of his enemies, looking like a slave.

theme.means: the open sea

herald.text: Scene 4. The Wooden Horse. Menelaus recalls the hollow wooden horse that smuggled Greek soldiers into the enemy city, and how Odysseus kept the hidden men silent.

greek.greek: ἦλθες ἔπειτα σὺ κεῖσε· κελευσέμεναι δέ σʼ ἔμελλε
greek.english: I crouched in that timber belly with the best of the Argives, and Odysseus held command of us all,

theme.means: a trick, a snare: the horse, the bed, the web Penelope weaves and unweaves

herald.text: Scene 5. Menelaus Wrestles Proteus. Menelaus tells how he wrestled a shape-changing sea god, who revealed that Odysseus is alive but held captive on a goddess's island.

greek.greek: γναμπτοῖς ἀγκίστροισιν, ἔτειρε δὲ γαστέρα λιμός.
greek.english: The gods held me windbound off Egypt, on the isle of Pharos, till hunger gnawed my crews —

theme.means: the homecoming. The Odyssey is the poem of one man's nostos; our word nostalgia is the ache for it

herald.text: Scene 6. The Gifts and the Eagle Omen. Telemachus insists on leaving; the royal couple give him gifts, and Helen reads an eagle seizing a goose as Odysseus's coming revenge.

greek.greek: καὶ τότε σʼ εὖ πέμψω, δώσω δέ τοι ἀγλαὰ δῶρα,
greek.english: Stay with me a month, Telemachus, and I will send you off with horses and a shining chariot —

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Scene 7. The Suitors Prepare an Ambush. On Ithaca, the suitors learn Telemachus has sailed and send a ship to ambush him; Penelope hears and collapses in fear.

greek.greek: οἴκαδε νισόμενον· ὁ δʼ ἔβη μετὰ πατρὸς ἀκουὴν
greek.english: the suitors plot to cut Telemachus down at sea as he sails home.

theme.means: glory, what is heard of a man: fame that outlives him in song

herald.text: Book 5. Odysseus—Nymph and Shipwreck. Now we meet Odysseus himself, held for years on a remote island by Calypso, a goddess who loves him and wants him to stay. The gods order her to let him go. He must cross the sea alone, and the sea god Poseidon still hates him. Scene 1. Hermes Carries the Decree. Zeus sends Hermes, the gods' messenger, flying over the sea to Calypso's island with the order to release Odysseus.

greek.greek: Ἑρμεία, σὺ γὰρ αὖτε τά τʼ ἄλλα περ ἄγγελός ἐσσι,
greek.english: Hermes, my son, our messenger as always —

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 2. Calypso Receives the Order. Calypso protests that the gods resent goddesses who love mortal men, but she agrees to let Odysseus go.

greek.greek: ἀλλʼ ἐπεὶ οὔ πως ἔστι Διὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο
greek.english: It was I who saved him when Zeus's bolt split his ship in the wine-dark sea —

theme.means: an oath, sworn on the gods

herald.text: Scene 3. Odysseus Distrusts Freedom. Odysseus suspects a trick until Calypso swears an oath; offered immortality with her, he still longs for his wife.

greek.greek: ἡ μὲν γὰρ βροτός ἐστι, σὺ δʼ ἀθάνατος καὶ ἀγήρως.
greek.english: wise Penelope must fade beside you, for she is mortal and you are deathless.

theme.means: the wife, she who shares the bed

herald.text: Scene 4. Building the Raft. With tools from Calypso, Odysseus builds a raft in four days, and she sends him off with food and a fair wind.

greek.greek: νήσου ἐπʼ ἐσχατιῆς, ὅθι δένδρεα μακρὰ πεφύκει,
greek.english: Here at the island's edge the tall trees stand —

herald.text: Scene 5. Poseidon Breaks the Sea. Poseidon wrecks the raft with a storm; Ino, a sea goddess, gives Odysseus a veil and tells him to swim.

greek.greek: ἔνθα κε δὴ δύστηνος ὑπὲρ μόρον ὤλετʼ Ὀδυσσεύς,
greek.english: Odysseus is swept away and barely regains it.

theme.means: grey-eyed, bright-eyed: Athena's epithet

herald.text: Scene 6. The River Accepts the Castaway. After two days swimming, Odysseus finds a calm river mouth, crawls ashore on an unknown land, and sleeps under leaves.

greek.greek: σόν τε ῥόον σά τε γούναθʼ ἱκάνω πολλὰ μογήσας.
greek.english: I come to your current a suppliant, fleeing Poseidon's anger out of the sea.

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Book 6. The Princess and the Stranger. Odysseus has washed up on Scheria, island of a rich seafaring people called the Phaeacians. Athena arranges for the king's daughter to find him. Everything depends on whether a stranger with nothing will be helped. Scene 1. Athena Enters Nausicaa's Dream. Athena appears in Princess Nausicaa's dream and urges her to wash clothes at the river, where Odysseus lies sleeping.

greek.greek: ὥπλεον, ἡμιόνους θʼ ὕπαγον ζεῦξάν θʼ ὑπʼ ἀπήνῃ·
greek.english: the servants will yoke the high wagon, the one with the box for the wash.

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 2. Laundry and Ball at the River. Nausicaa and her maids wash clothes and play ball by the river; their shout wakes Odysseus.

greek.greek: μάστιξεν δʼ ἐλάαν· καναχὴ δʼ ἦν ἡμιόνοιιν.
greek.english: Nausicaa and her maids drive to the washing pools, unharness the mules, and tread the clothes clean.

theme.means: grey-eyed, bright-eyed: Athena's epithet

herald.text: Scene 3. The Naked Stranger Emerges. Naked and salt-caked, Odysseus covers himself with a branch and begs Nausicaa for help; her maids flee but she stands firm.

greek.greek: ξεῖνʼ, ἐπεὶ οὔτε κακῷ οὔτʼ ἄφρονι φωτὶ ἔοικας·
greek.english: Stranger, you seem neither base nor witless, and Zeus deals fortune as he wills —

theme.means: the open sea

herald.text: Scene 4. Bath, Clothing, and the Road to Town. Washed and dressed, Odysseus looks splendid; Nausicaa tells him to follow her to town and plead first with the queen.

greek.greek: δήεις ἀγλαὸν ἄλσος Ἀθήνης ἄγχι κελεύθου
greek.english: but when we near the town, wait in Athena's grove of poplars until you judge we have reached my father's house,

theme.means: a fool, a child: the one who does not see what is coming

herald.text: Book 7. Phaeacia's Halls and Gardens. Following the princess's advice, Odysseus walks into the Phaeacian city, hidden by a mist Athena wraps around him. He must win over the king and queen without revealing who he is. These people could carry him home by ship. Scene 1. Athena Hides the Walk through Scheria. Disguised as a girl carrying water, Athena guides the hidden Odysseus through the city and tells him to seek out Queen Arete.

greek.greek: δέσποιναν μὲν πρῶτα κιχήσεαι ἐν μεγάροισιν·
greek.english: Go straight through the hall to the queen, Arete, whom the people honor like a god.

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 2. The Palace and the Gardens. Odysseus stands amazed before the king's palace, with its golden doors and an orchard that bears fruit all year.

greek.greek: ἀργύρεον δʼ ἐφʼ ὑπερθύριον, χρυσέη δὲ κορώνη.
greek.english: Walls of bronze, and doors of gold on silver posts —

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 3. Supplication at Arete's Knees. Odysseus kneels before Queen Arete and begs for passage home; after a long silence, the king raises him and promises a ship.

greek.greek: σόν τε πόσιν σά τε γούναθʼ ἱκάνω πολλὰ μογήσας
greek.english: Arete, daughter of Rhexenor, after many trials I come to your knees, and to your king,

theme.means: glory, what is heard of a man: fame that outlives him in song

herald.text: Scene 4. Arete Recognizes Her Work. The queen recognizes the clothes he wears; Odysseus tells of his shipwreck without giving his name, and King Alcinous promises him passage.

greek.greek: ἔνθα μὲν ἑπτάετες μένον ἔμπεδον, εἵματα δʼ αἰεὶ
greek.english: Far off lies an island where the goddess Calypso held me seven years against my will,

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Book 8. A Day for Songs and Contests. The Phaeacians hold a day of feasting, games, and songs for their unknown guest. A blind singer performs stories of the war at Troy, and some of them are about Odysseus himself. The guest's tears begin to give him away. Scene 1. The Phaeacian Assembly and the Ship. Athena calls the people together and makes Odysseus look impressive; the king orders a ship and crew made ready for him.

greek.greek: παίσατε, ὥς χʼ ὁ ξεῖνος ἐνίσπῃ οἷσι φίλοισιν
greek.english: To assembly, captains and counselors of the Phaeacians!

herald.text: Scene 2. Demodocus Sings of the Quarrel. The blind singer Demodocus sings of the war at Troy, and Odysseus secretly weeps into his cloak; only the king notices.

greek.greek: νεῖκος Ὀδυσσῆος καὶ Πηλεΐδεω Ἀχιλῆος,
greek.english: Odysseus and Achilles, best of the Achaeans, at strife with high words at the gods' rich feast!

theme.means: the singer, the bard: the poem's own maker inside the poem

herald.text: Scene 3. The Athletic Challenge. At the games a young man named Euryalus mocks the stranger, and Odysseus answers by throwing a discus farther than anyone.

greek.greek: ἄφρων δὴ κεῖνός γε καὶ οὐτιδανὸς πέλει ἀνήρ,
greek.english: Now let any Phaeacian but Laodamas, my host's son, come and try me —

theme.means: a sign, a token, a grave-marker: the scar and the bed are sēmata by which Odysseus is known

herald.text: Scene 4. The Dance and the Net of Hephaestus. Demodocus sings of two gods caught in a net, dancers perform, and Euryalus apologizes with the gift of a sword.

greek.greek: εὕδειν ἐν λέκτροισι παρὰ χρυσέῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ;
greek.english: Hear now how Ares and golden Aphrodite lay together in secret,

theme.means: shame, reverence: the sense that stops a man from doing wrong before others and the gods

herald.text: Scene 5. The Trojan Horse Song and the Name. Odysseus asks for the song of the wooden horse, weeps again, and the king finally demands to know his name and story.

greek.greek: ὡς ἄρα τοι πρόφρων θεὸς ὤπασε θέσπιν ἀοιδήν.
words: filled with the words of God
greek.english: Now shift your ground and sing the wooden horse, the trap Epeius built with Athena,

theme.means: a trick, a snare: the horse, the bed, the web Penelope weaves and unweaves

herald.text: Book 9. In the One-Eyed Giant's Cave. Odysseus names himself to the Phaeacians and begins to tell his story, so from here the film shows his memories of the years after the war. He left Troy with twelve ships full of men. This is how he started losing them, beginning with a giant's cave. Scene 1. Odysseus Names Himself. At last Odysseus tells the court his name, says his home is Ithaca, and begins the story of his journey.

greek.greek: ἥμεθα δαινύμενοι κρέα τʼ ἄσπετα καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
greek.english: feasters ranged down the hall listening, the tables full of bread and meat, the steward pouring wine.

theme.means: rosy-fingered: the dawn's epithet, the formula that opens a new day

herald.text: Scene 2. The Raid on the Cicones. Leaving Troy, his men raid a town and linger to feast against his orders, until the townspeople strike back and kill many.

greek.greek: ὥς οἱ ὑπʼ εἰροπόκων ὀίων στέρνοισι δέδεντο.
greek.english: The sheep are fat and the wine runs dark and sweet —

theme.means: a fool, a child: the one who does not see what is coming

herald.text: Scene 3. The Lotus-Eaters. Some sailors eat the lotus, a plant that makes them forget home; Odysseus drags them weeping back to the ships.

greek.greek: μή πώς τις λωτοῖο φαγὼν νόστοιο λάθηται.
greek.english: The rest of you aboard and to your oars now, before another man tastes the lotus and forgets his home.

theme.means: the homecoming. The Odyssey is the poem of one man's nostos; our word nostalgia is the ache for it

herald.text: Scene 4. Goat Island and the Cyclops Coast. The fleet rests on an island near the land of the one-eyed giants, and Odysseus takes one ship to explore.

greek.greek: νῆσος ἔπειτα λάχεια παρὲκ λιμένος τετάνυσται,
greek.english: The fleet comes then to a wooded island where wild goats breed and no plow has ever cut,

theme.means: the wife, she who shares the bed

herald.text: Scene 5. The Empty Cave. Odysseus and twelve men find a cave full of food; the men want to steal and run, but he insists on waiting.

greek.greek: καρπαλίμως ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν ἐρίφους τε καὶ ἄρνας
greek.english: Let us take the cheeses and drive the lambs and kids to the ship, they begged him —

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 6. Polyphemus Seals the Cave. The giant Polyphemus comes home, seals the cave with a huge stone, and discovers the strangers hiding inside.

greek.greek: τὸν δʼ ἐπιμασσάμενος προσέφη κρατερὸς Πολύφημος·
greek.english: At dusk Polyphemus returns carrying a massive load of wood and drives his flock inside.

theme.means: Nobody: the name Odysseus gives the Cyclops, and a pun on mētis, cunning

herald.text: Scene 7. The First Killings. Odysseus asks for the kindness owed to guests, but Polyphemus scorns the gods and eats two of his men.

greek.greek: ὣς ἔφαθʼ, ἡμῖν δʼ αὖτε κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ,
greek.english: We are Achaeans out of Troy, men of Agamemnon, whose fame is the widest now under heaven —

theme.means: the open sea

herald.text: Scene 8. The Name Nobody and the Stake. Trapped, Odysseus sharpens a wooden stake in secret, then gives the giant strong wine and tells him his name is Nobody.

greek.greek: Κύκλωψ, τῆ, πίε οἶνον, ἐπεὶ φάγες ἀνδρόμεα κρέα,
greek.english: drink wine on that man-flesh you have eaten, and learn what drink our ship carried.

theme.means: cunning intelligence, the craft of the mind. Odysseus's own gift, and Athena's

herald.text: Scene 9. The Blinding. They drive the burning stake into the giant's eye; when neighbors come, he shouts that Nobody is hurting him, so they leave.

greek.greek: ἦ μή τίς σʼ αὐτὸν κτείνει δόλῳ ἠὲ βίηφιν;
greek.english: What ails you, Polyphemus, that you wake the deathless night with screaming —

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 10. Escape beneath the Rams. The men escape by clinging to the bellies of sheep as the blind giant lets his flock out to graze.

greek.greek: ὥς οἱ ὑπʼ εἰροπόκων ὀίων στέρνοισι δέδεντο.
greek.english: I took the great lead ram myself and hung beneath his belly, my hands twisted in that miracle of wool,

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Scene 11. The Boast and the Curse. Safe on the water, Odysseus boasts his real name; Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon to make the homecoming late and lonely.

greek.greek: χειρῶν ἐξ Ὀδυσῆος ἁμαρτήσεσθαι ὀπωπῆς.
greek.english: Telemus foretold I would lose my sight at the hands of Odysseus, and I watched all these years for a great man,

theme.means: a trick, a snare: the horse, the bed, the web Penelope weaves and unweaves

herald.text: Book 10. The Bewitching Queen of Aeaea. Odysseus continues his story to the Phaeacians. Home comes within sight and is lost, most of his fleet is destroyed, and the survivors land on the island of a powerful enchantress. To go on, he must learn to bargain with her. Scene 1. Aeolus and the Bag of Winds. Aeolus bottles the bad winds in a bag; within sight of home, the crew opens it and the winds blow them back.

greek.greek: ἔνθα δὲ βυκτάων ἀνέμων κατέδησε κέλευθα·
greek.english: I loose the West Wind only;

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 2. The Laestrygonian Harbor. Cannibal giants hurl boulders into a harbor and destroy every ship but Odysseus's own, which was moored outside.

greek.greek: αὐτὰρ ὁ τεῦχε βοὴν διὰ ἄστεος· οἱ δʼ ἀίοντες
greek.english: Then the Laestrygonians came in thousands, giants and not men.

theme.means: rosy-fingered: the dawn's epithet, the formula that opens a new day

herald.text: Scene 3. Scouts on Aeaea. On a new island the survivors rest, and Eurylochus leads half the men inland toward a house where smoke is rising.

greek.greek: βῆ δʼ ἰέναι, ἅμα τῷ γε δύω καὶ εἴκοσʼ ἑταῖροι
greek.english: Eurylochus leads one and I the other —

theme.means: the wife, she who shares the bed

herald.text: Scene 4. Circe Transforms the Crew. Circe welcomes the men with drugged food and turns them into pigs; only Eurylochus stays outside and runs back to warn Odysseus.

greek.greek: διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχανʼ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
greek.english: They are gone, Odysseus —

theme.means: of many turns: the first epithet of Odysseus, the man of many ways and many wanderings

herald.text: Scene 5. Hermes Gives the Moly. Going alone to rescue them, Odysseus meets Hermes, who gives him a magic herb that will protect him from Circe's drug.

greek.greek: εἰ μή μοι τλαίης γε, θεά, μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμόσσαι
greek.english: And before you go to her bed, make her swear the great oath of the gods that she plots no further harm —

theme.means: reckless folly, the arrogance that brings its own ruin: the crews', the suitors'

herald.text: Scene 6. Odysseus Defeats Circe's Spell. Circe's spell fails on Odysseus; he draws his sword, and she swears an oath to do him no harm.

greek.greek: ἦ σύ γʼ Ὀδυσσεύς ἐσσι πολύτροπος, ὅν τέ μοι αἰεὶ
greek.english: You are Odysseus —

theme.means: an oath, sworn on the gods

herald.text: Scene 7. The Men Restored. Circe turns the pigs back into men; the whole crew stays with her for a year before they ask to go home.

greek.greek: βῆν δʼ ἰέναι ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης.
greek.english: Haul the ship high and follow me —

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 8. The Road to the Dead. Circe says Odysseus must first consult a prophet in the land of the dead; Elpenor falls from a roof and dies unnoticed.

greek.greek: ὣς ἔφαν, αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γʼ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
greek.english: Circe, keep now the promise that you made me:

theme.means: the homecoming. The Odyssey is the poem of one man's nostos; our word nostalgia is the ache for it

herald.text: Book 11. The Kingdom of the Dead. Still telling his story, Odysseus describes his journey to the land of the dead. He goes to ask a dead prophet how to get home. There he also meets the ghosts of people he loved and soldiers he fought beside. Scene 1. The Blood Pit Opens. At the edge of the world, Odysseus pours blood into a pit, and the ghosts of the dead swarm to drink.

greek.greek: ἔνθα δὲ Κιμμερίων ἀνδρῶν δῆμός τε πόλις τε,
greek.english: The ship came to deep-flowing Ocean's edge, to the land of the Cimmerians, wrapped in mist and cloud,

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 2. Elpenor Asks for Burial. The first ghost is Elpenor, who begs Odysseus to go back and give his body a proper burial.

greek.greek: εἰς ὅ κε τοὺς ἀφίκηαι οἳ οὐκ ἴσασι θάλασσαν
greek.english: Burn me with all my armor and heap a mound by the grey sea, for an unlucky man that men to come may know of.

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Scene 3. Tiresias Names the Cost. The prophet Tiresias warns that the crew must not touch the Sun god's cattle, and that Odysseus will reach home alone.

greek.greek: εἰ δέ κε σίνηαι, τότε τοι τεκμαίρομʼ ὄλεθρον,
greek.english: Harm them, and I foretell ruin for ship and crew —

theme.means: a sign, a token, a grave-marker: the scar and the bed are sēmata by which Odysseus is known

herald.text: Scene 4. Anticleia and the Three Embraces. Odysseus meets his mother, who died of longing for him; three times he tries to hug her, and his arms pass through.

greek.greek: σὸν δʼ οὔ πώ τις ἔχει καλὸν γέρας, ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος
greek.english: longing for me, for my counsels and my gentleness —

theme.means: the open sea

herald.text: Scene 5. The Heroines of the Past. A procession of famous women from old stories rises to drink the blood and tell who they were.

greek.greek: καί ῥʼ ἔτεκεν δύο παῖδʼ, Ἀμφίονά τε Ζῆθόν τε,
greek.english: Then came Antiope and Alcmene, Megara and sorrowing Epicaste, Chloris, Leda, Iphimedeia, Phaedra, Ariadne —

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 6. Agamemnon's Warning. Agamemnon's ghost tells how his wife and her lover murdered him on his homecoming, and warns Odysseus to return in secret.

greek.greek: Ἀτρεΐδη, τί με ταῦτα διείρεαι; οὐδέ τι οἶδα,
greek.english: About Orestes, but Odysseus has no news?

theme.means: the singer, the bard: the poem's own maker inside the poem

herald.text: Scene 7. Achilles Chooses Life in Retrospect. Achilles says death holds no glory, asks after his family, and strides off rejoicing to hear his son fought bravely.

greek.greek: βουλοίμην κʼ ἐπάρουρος ἐὼν θητευέμεν ἄλλῳ,
greek.english: Achilles, no man was ever more blessed, nor will be:

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Scene 8. Judges, Punishments, and Flight. Odysseus sees the punished dead and famous heroes, until the crowding ghosts frighten him back to his ship.

greek.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν αὐτοῦ μένον ἔμπεδον, εἴ τις ἔτʼ ἔλθοι
greek.english: Son of Zeus I was, and still I slaved for a lesser man, who sent me down even here to drag away the hound.

theme.means: grey-eyed, bright-eyed: Athena's epithet

herald.text: Book 12. The Cattle of the Sun. Odysseus finishes his story with the last stage of the voyage. Circe warns him of the dangers ahead, and he faces them one by one. The worst danger turns out to be his own hungry crew. Scene 1. Elpenor's Funeral. Back on Circe's island, the crew burns Elpenor's body and plants his oar on the grave, as promised.

greek.greek: νηῦς, ἀπὸ δʼ ἵκετο κῦμα θαλάσσης εὐρυπόροιο
greek.english: At dawn they fetched Elpenor's body from Circe's roof, and wept, and burned him with all his armor,

theme.means: rosy-fingered: the dawn's epithet, the formula that opens a new day

herald.text: Scene 2. Circe Maps the Dangers. Circe privately describes each danger ahead and how to survive it, and warns Odysseus not to fight what cannot be fought.

greek.greek: ἀνθρώπους θέλγουσιν, ὅτις σφεας εἰσαφίκηται.
greek.english: First the Sirens, who enchant every man that comes near them;

theme.means: a fool, a child: the one who does not see what is coming

herald.text: Scene 3. The Sirens' Song. Odysseus plugs his men's ears with wax and has them tie him to the mast, so he can hear the Sirens safely.

greek.greek: ἀλλʼ ὅτε δὴ τὴν νῆσον ἐλείπομεν, οὐδέ τις ἄλλη
greek.english: and the crew rowed until the song sank beneath the sound of the sea.

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 4. Between Scylla and Charybdis. Avoiding a deadly whirlpool, they row close to the opposite cliff, where the monster Scylla snatches six men from the ship.

greek.greek: ἦ τοι ὅτʼ ἐξεμέσειε, λέβης ὣς ἐν πυρὶ πολλῷ
greek.english: Helmsman, hold her off that smoke and hug the cliff —

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 5. The Island of the Sun. On the island of the Sun god's cattle, the men swear not to touch them, but storms trap them for a month.

greek.greek: σχέτλιός εἰς, Ὀδυσεῦ· περί τοι μένος, οὐδέ τι γυῖα
greek.english: Call me merciless if you will, Eurylochus —

theme.means: a trick, a snare: the horse, the bed, the web Penelope weaves and unweaves

herald.text: Scene 6. The Cattle Are Slaughtered. While Odysseus sleeps, Eurylochus persuades the starving men to kill the sacred cattle; the Sun god demands revenge from Zeus.

greek.greek: ἠδʼ ὁπότʼ ἂψ ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἀπʼ οὐρανόθεν προτραποίμην.
greek.english: Lampetie tells Helios, who demands punishment from Zeus.

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 7. Zeus Destroys the Last Ship. Zeus strikes the ship with lightning and every man drowns; Odysseus alone clings to the wreck and drifts to Calypso's island.

greek.greek: Ζεῦ πάτερ ἠδʼ ἄλλοι μάκαρες θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες,
greek.english: O father Zeus, you lulled me to my ruin.

theme.means: the homecoming. The Odyssey is the poem of one man's nostos; our word nostalgia is the ache for it

herald.text: Book 13. Ithaca at Last. Odysseus, king of the island of Ithaca, has been away twenty years: ten at war, ten lost at sea. Now a friendly people finally ship him home, but his house is overrun by men who court his wife and eat his wealth. He must come back in secret. Scene 1. The Phaeacians Carry Odysseus Home. A friendly seafaring people sail the sleeping king home by night and leave him and his gifts on Ithaca's shore.

greek.greek: ἀσπασίως δʼ ἄρα τῷ κατέδυ φάος ἠελίοιο
greek.english: Then set the feast, for our guest sails at sundown and he must leave us glad.

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 2. Odysseus Wakes on an Unknown Shore. Odysseus wakes in mist, does not recognize his own island, and fears he has been abandoned in a strange land.

greek.greek: ἀλλὰ σάω μὲν ταῦτα, σάω δʼ ἐμέ· σοὶ γὰρ ἐγώ γε
greek.english: Stranger, why do you wander this coast with treasure at your feet and fear in your eyes?

theme.means: grey-eyed, bright-eyed: Athena's epithet

herald.text: Scene 3. The Cretan Lie Meets Its Match. The goddess, disguised as a shepherd, tells him he is home; he lies about who he is, and she reveals herself.

greek.greek: Παλλάδʼ Ἀθηναίην, κούρην Διός, ἥ τέ τοι αἰεὶ
words: coin bearing the head of Pallas
greek.english: I am Athena, daughter of Zeus, and we two are alike, crooked-minded both,

theme.means: glory, what is heard of a man: fame that outlives him in song

herald.text: Scene 4. The Treasure Is Hidden. Athena helps him hide his treasure in a cave and plan against the suitors; first he must go to his swineherd.

greek.greek: ἐς Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν ἔβη μετὰ παῖδʼ Ὀδυσῆος.
greek.english: I go to Sparta, to fetch your son home.

theme.means: cunning intelligence, the craft of the mind. Odysseus's own gift, and Athena's

herald.text: Scene 5. Athena Makes the Beggar. The goddess turns the king into a ragged old beggar so he can test his household without being recognized.

greek.greek: ἀμφὶ δέ μιν μέγα δέρμα ταχείης ἕσσʼ ἐλάφοιο,
greek.english: Dimmed eyes, wracked limbs, rags fit for burning on an old man's back.

theme.means: the wife, she who shares the bed

herald.text: Book 14. The Loyal Swineherd. Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus reaches the farm of his old swineherd. Before trusting anyone, he must learn who is still loyal to him. Scene 1. The Dogs at Eumaeus's Yard. Fierce dogs attack the disguised king at the swineherd's farm until Eumaeus drives them off and welcomes the stranger.

greek.greek: καὶ δέ μοι ἄλλα θεοὶ δόσαν ἄλγεά τε στοναχάς τε·
greek.english: Out of the yard four dogs came at him like wolves, and the man dropped his staff and sat down in the dirt,

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Scene 2. The Swineherd Laments His Master. The swineherd curses the suitors eating his master's herds; the beggar swears Odysseus will return, but Eumaeus will not believe it.

greek.greek: ἤπιον ὧδε ἄνακτα κιχήσομαι, ὁππόσʼ ἐπέλθω,
greek.english: My master, and I will say his name, Odysseus, was kind to me past any telling, and the sea has him now,

theme.means: an oath, sworn on the gods

herald.text: Scene 3. The Cretan Tale at the Hut. The disguised king tells a long invented life story, testing how much the swineherd will believe.

greek.greek: οἴκαδε νοστήσει, καὶ τίσεται ὅς τις ἐκείνου
greek.english: And this Thesprotian king, say again what he swore to you about Odysseus and the treasure coming home.

theme.means: the open sea

herald.text: Scene 4. The Cloak Test. On a cold night, the beggar hints with a story that he needs a cloak, and the swineherd generously lends one.

greek.greek: ὡς ὅθʼ ὑπὸ Τροίην λόχον ἤγομεν ἀρτύναντες.
greek.english: One freezing ambush-night at Troy I lay without a cloak,

theme.means: shame, reverence: the sense that stops a man from doing wrong before others and the gods

herald.text: Book 15. The Prince Sets Sail for Home. Far away in the kingdom of Sparta, Odysseus's son has been searching for news of his father. The goddess sends him home, warning that the suitors are waiting to kill him at sea. Meanwhile, the disguised king waits at the swineherd's hut. Scene 1. Athena Wakes Telemachus. In Sparta, the goddess warns the king's son to sail home at once and avoid the suitors' ambush.

greek.greek: τοὺς δʼ Ἰθάκῃ ἐπέλασσε φέρων ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕδωρ,
greek.english: the boldest of the suitors lie in ambush in the strait between Ithaca and rocky Same,

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 2. Farewell from Menelaus and Helen. The son leaves the king and queen of Sparta with gifts; a bird sign suggests his father's revenge is near.

greek.greek: Τηλέμαχʼ, ἦ τοι νόστον, ὅπως φρεσὶ σῇσι μενοινᾷς,
greek.english: Menelaus, dear to Zeus, your gifts honor me and I take them gladly.

theme.means: rosy-fingered: the dawn's epithet, the formula that opens a new day

herald.text: Scene 3. Theoclymenus Joins the Voyage. At the harbor, the son takes aboard a fugitive prophet and sails through the night toward Ithaca.

greek.greek: Τηλεμάχου ἕταροι λύον ἱστία, κὰδ δʼ ἕλον ἱστὸν
greek.english: Aboard, men, rig the mast and run out the oars.

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Scene 4. Eumaeus Tells His Own Story. At the hut, the swineherd tells the beggar how he was kidnapped as a child and raised in Odysseus's family.

greek.greek: Λαέρτης μὲν ἔτι ζώει, Διὶ δʼ εὔχεται αἰεὶ
greek.english: Tell me of old Laertes, does he still live?

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 5. Telemachus Lands in Secret. A hawk kills a dove, which the prophet reads as good news; the son lands secretly and walks toward the swineherd's farm.

greek.greek: ὅρκῳ πιστωθῆναι ἀπήμονά μʼ οἴκαδʼ ἀπάξειν.
greek.english: Crew, take her round to the town harbor without me;

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Book 16. Father and Son. Father and son, who have not seen each other in twenty years, are about to meet in the swineherd's hut. The son does not know the beggar is his father. Scene 1. The Son Reaches the Hut. The son reaches the hut; the swineherd weeps with joy, and the disguised father offers his seat.

greek.greek: ἢ αὐτοῦ παρʼ ἐμοί τε μένῃ καὶ δῶμα κομίζῃ,
greek.english: For news and enters the hut beside the unknown beggar?

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 2. Eumaeus Carries News to Penelope. The swineherd leaves to tell the queen her son is safe, and the goddess signals Odysseus that he may reveal himself.

greek.greek: εἴφʼ ὅτι οἱ σῶς εἰμὶ καὶ ἐκ Πύλου εἰλήλουθα.
greek.english: Eumaeus to report your safe return to Penelope privately?

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 3. The Father Reveals Himself. Restored to his true form, Odysseus tells his son who he is; after doubt, they embrace and weep.

greek.greek: τὸν δʼ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
greek.english: Himself the father for whom Telemachus has suffered.

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 4. The Plan against the Suitors. Father and son count the suitors and plan to hide the palace weapons, telling no one, not even the queen.

greek.greek: καὶ φράσαι ἤ κεν νῶϊν Ἀθήνη σὺν Διὶ πατρὶ
greek.english: Zeus and Athena stand with us, and they are worth more than a hundred spears.

theme.means: the singer, the bard: the poem's own maker inside the poem

herald.text: Scene 5. The Ambush Fails and the Suitors Divide. The suitors learn the son escaped their ambush; Antinous urges murder, and the queen confronts them.

greek.greek: νῆα παρερχομένην, τὴν δʼ οὐκ ἐδύναντο κιχῆναι.
greek.english: Telemachus's ship reaches harbor before the ambush vessel can intercept it.

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 6. The Beggar Returns. The goddess makes Odysseus a beggar again before the swineherd returns, and father and son keep their secret.

greek.greek: νῆα παρερχομένην, τὴν δʼ οὐκ ἐδύναντο κιχῆναι.
greek.english: Telemachus's safe arrival and the suitors' failed ship.

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Book 17. Stranger at the Gates. The disguised king walks into his own palace for the first time in twenty years. He must endure insults from the suitors without giving himself away. Scene 1. Telemachus Returns to the Palace. The son returns to the palace and greets his mother but hides his father's return; the prophet says Odysseus is already here.

greek.greek: νόστον σοῦ πατρὸς σάφα εἰπέμεν, εἴ που ἄκουσας.
greek.english: What Nestor and Menelaus told him but withholds the plan and his father's return.

theme.means: the homecoming. The Odyssey is the poem of one man's nostos; our word nostalgia is the ache for it

herald.text: Scene 2. The Road with Melanthius. On the road to town, a goatherd who serves the suitors kicks and insults the beggar, who holds back his anger.

greek.greek: σίγα, μή μοι τοῦτον ἀμείβεο πολλὰ ἔπεσσιν·
greek.english: Is that the best you can offer, Eumaeus?

theme.means: the open sea

herald.text: Scene 3. Argos Recognizes His Master. Odysseus's old dog, neglected for twenty years, recognizes his master's voice, wags his tail, and dies.

greek.greek: δὴ τότε γʼ, ὡς ἐνόησεν Ὀδυσσέα ἐγγὺς ἐόντα,
greek.english: Near the palace Odysseus sees his old dog Argos lying neglected on dung.

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 4. The Beggar Enters His Hall. The disguised king enters his own hall and begs from each suitor to learn which of them are decent.

greek.greek: δός οἱ ἑλών· οὔ τοι φθονέω· κέλομαι γὰρ ἐγώ γε·
greek.english: Give what you can spare, my lord.

theme.means: shame, reverence: the sense that stops a man from doing wrong before others and the gods

herald.text: Scene 5. Antinous Throws the Stool. Antinous insults the beggar and hits him with a footstool, breaking the rule that strangers must be protected.

greek.greek: Ἀντίνοον πρὸ γάμοιο τέλος θανάτοιο κιχείη.
greek.english: Let Antinous meet his death before his wedding day.

theme.means: a fool, a child: the one who does not see what is coming

herald.text: Scene 6. Penelope Summons the Stranger. The queen asks to meet the stranger; he waits until evening, and her son's sneeze seems to promise the suitors' deaths.

greek.greek: καλὸς μὲν δέμας ἐστίν, ἀτὰρ τόδε γʼ οὐ σάφα οἶδα,
greek.english: Eumaeus to bring him for questioning?

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Scene 7. Eumaeus Leaves the Hall. The swineherd returns to his farm, leaving the disguised king alone in the palace among the suitors.

greek.greek: ᾠχόμεθʼ ἔς τε Πύλον καὶ Νέστορα, ποιμένα λαῶν·
greek.english: Come back at dawn with news.

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Book 18. The Beggar-King of Ithaca. The disguised king stays in his own hall among the suitors. They treat him as entertainment, and he quietly measures each of them. Scene 1. Irus Challenges the Stranger. A local beggar tries to chase Odysseus from the door, and the amused suitors push the two into a fight.

greek.greek: ἦλθε δʼ ἐπὶ πτωχὸς πανδήμιος, ὃς κατὰ ἄστυ
greek.english: There is room for only one beggar here.

herald.text: Scene 2. Odysseus Drops Irus. Odysseus reveals his strength and knocks the other beggar down with one blow, careful not to kill him.

greek.greek: ὣς φάτο, καὶ σπείσας ἔπιεν μελιηδέα οἶνον,
greek.english: Cheer and Amphinomus gives the victor food and wine.

theme.means: grey-eyed, bright-eyed: Athena's epithet

herald.text: Scene 3. The Warning to Amphinomus. The beggar warns the kindest suitor that the king will soon return; Amphinomus is shaken but stays.

greek.greek: τῷ μή τίς ποτε πάμπαν ἀνὴρ ἀθεμίστιος εἴη,
greek.english: no man should become lawless in prosperity.

theme.means: glory, what is heard of a man: fame that outlives him in song

herald.text: Scene 4. Penelope Appears before the Suitors. The queen appears before the suitors and shames them into bringing her gifts, while her disguised husband silently admires her cleverness.

greek.greek: Τηλέμαχʼ, οὐκέτι τοι φρένες ἔμπεδοι οὐδὲ νόημα·
greek.english: Telemachus, your mind was steadier when you were a boy.

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 5. Melantho and Eurymachus Attack. A disloyal maid and Eurymachus mock the beggar; Eurymachus throws a stool, and the son ends the night.

greek.greek: ταρβεῖς· ἦ ῥά σε οἶνος ἔχει φρένας, ἤ νύ τοι αἰεὶ
greek.english: The poor thing has had one cup of wine and now he is a prophet.

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Book 19. Penelope and Her Guest. At night, with the suitors gone, the king and his son hide the weapons. Then the queen sits down to question the beggar, not knowing he is her husband. Scene 1. The Weapons Leave the Hall. Father and son secretly carry the weapons out of the hall, leaving the suitors unarmed for what is coming.

greek.greek: καλά, τά μοι κατὰ οἶκον ἀκηδέα καπνὸς ἀμέρδει
greek.english: Tells Eurycleia the smoke has damaged them and you must be protected from drunken quarrels.

theme.means: a fool, a child: the one who does not see what is coming

herald.text: Scene 2. Penelope Begins the Test. The queen questions the beggar, tells how she has stalled the suitors for years, and asks proof that he knew her husband.

greek.greek: ἤ τίς που καὶ ξεῖνος, ἐπεὶ πολλοῖσιν Ὀδυσσεὺς
greek.english: For proof that the stranger truly knows Odysseus?

theme.means: a trick, a snare: the horse, the bed, the web Penelope weaves and unweaves

herald.text: Scene 3. The Stranger Describes Odysseus. The beggar describes her husband's clothes exactly; she weeps, while he hides his own grief and promises Odysseus is near.

greek.greek: οὔτʼ Ὀδυσεὺς ἔτι οἶκον ἐλεύσεται, οὔτε σὺ πομπῆς
greek.english: swears Odysseus is near and will return within the month.

theme.means: a sign, a token, a grave-marker: the scar and the bed are sēmata by which Odysseus is known

herald.text: Scene 4. Eurycleia Finds the Scar. Washing the beggar's feet, the old nurse feels a childhood scar and knows him; he forces her to stay silent.

greek.greek: νίψον σοῖο ἄνακτος ὁμήλικα· καί που Ὀδυσσεὺς
greek.english: Eurycleia, rise and wash the feet of your master's age-mate.

theme.means: cunning intelligence, the craft of the mind. Odysseus's own gift, and Athena's

herald.text: Scene 5. The Boar Hunt on Parnassus. A memory: young Odysseus is gored by a wild boar while hunting, which left the scar the nurse just found.

greek.greek: οὐλὴν ὅττι πάθοι· ὁ δʼ ἄρα σφίσιν εὖ κατέλεξεν
greek.english: The scar triggers the story of young Odysseus visiting his grandfather Autolycus.

theme.means: rosy-fingered: the dawn's epithet, the formula that opens a new day

herald.text: Scene 6. The Dream of the Geese. The queen tells a dream of an eagle killing geese, then announces a contest: she will marry whoever masters Odysseus's bow.

greek.greek: πρὶν γάρ τοι πολύμητις ἐλεύσεται ἐνθάδʼ Ὀδυσσεύς,
greek.english: she will marry the man who strings Odysseus's bow and shoots through twelve axes.

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Book 20. Portents Gather. It is the night before the contest. The king lies awake, unsure he can defeat so many men, while the gods send warning signs of what is coming. Scene 1. The Restless Night. Odysseus lies awake, angry and doubtful, until the goddess promises to protect him; upstairs the queen dreams of her husband.

greek.greek: τόφρʼ οὔ τις νέμεσις μενέμεν τʼ ἦν ἰσχέμεναί τε
greek.english: Hear me, for death, and dreams that Odysseus lies beside her.

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 2. Thunder and the Mill Woman. Odysseus asks the gods for a sign; thunder sounds from a clear sky, and a tired servant prays for the suitors' end.

greek.greek: ἔνδοθεν, ἔκτοσθεν δὲ Διὸς τέρας ἄλλο φανήτω.
greek.english: Zeus for a double sign from sky and household?

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Scene 3. The Herdsmen Arrive. Herdsmen arrive for a festival: the goatherd insults the beggar, but a loyal cowherd greets him warmly.

greek.greek: νοστῆσαι Ὀδυσῆα πολύφρονα ὅνδε δόμονδε.
greek.english: Before you drive your cattle home again, Odysseus will stand in this house,

theme.means: an oath, sworn on the gods

herald.text: Scene 4. The Ox Hoof. A suitor throws an ox hoof at the beggar; the son warns he will kill the next man who attacks his guest.

greek.greek: μοῖραν μὲν δὴ ξεῖνος ἔχει πάλαι, ὡς ἐπέοικεν,
greek.english: Is that the best you can offer, the beggar and hurls an ox hoof as a guest-gift?

theme.means: a fool, a child: the one who does not see what is coming

herald.text: Scene 5. The Hall of Death. The suitors laugh wildly while the prophet sees them covered in blood and shadow, and warns they are doomed.

greek.greek: Τηλέμαχος, φίλος υἱὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο.
greek.english: Telemachus and Odysseus watch one another across the doomed feast.

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Book 21. Odysseus Strings His Bow. The queen brings out her absent husband's great bow. Whoever can string it and shoot through twelve axes will marry her. Scene 1. Penelope Retrieves the Bow. The queen takes her husband's great bow from the storeroom, weeps over it, and brings it to the suitors.

greek.greek: ἐς δʼ ἄρα καὶ τὼ δμῶε ἴτην θείου Ὀδυσῆος.
greek.english: The queen enters the storeroom, unlocks the doors, and lifts Odysseus's bow and quiver down.

theme.means: reckless folly, the arrogance that brings its own ruin: the crews', the suitors'

herald.text: Scene 2. The Contest Is Set. The queen announces the contest; her son nearly strings the bow himself, until his father signals him to stop.

greek.greek: οὐ γάρ τις μέτα τοῖος ἀνὴρ ἐν τοίσδεσι πᾶσιν
greek.english: Here is the great bow of Odysseus.

theme.means: the wife, she who shares the bed

herald.text: Scene 3. The Suitors Fail the Bow. One suitor after another fails to bend the bow, and the shamed suitors postpone the contest.

greek.greek: ἄγρει δή, πῦρ κῆον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι, Μελανθεῦ,
greek.english: Melanthius lights a fire and brings fat so the bow can be warmed and greased.

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 4. Odysseus Recruits the Herdsmen. Outside, Odysseus shows his scar to the two loyal herdsmen, reveals who he is, and gives them their tasks.

greek.greek: σοὶ δέ, Φιλοίτιε δῖε, θύρας ἐπιτέλλομαι αὐλῆς
greek.english: Assigns Eumaeus to deliver the bow, Philoetius to lock the courtyard gate, and both to secure the women.

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Scene 5. The Beggar Requests the Bow. The beggar asks to try the bow; the suitors rage, the son sends his mother upstairs, and the swineherd delivers it.

greek.greek: καὶ καθάπαξ ξείνῳ δόμεναι τάδε τόξα φέρεσθαι.
greek.english: Let the stranger have the bow.

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 6. The Doors Are Secured. The nurse locks the women away and the cowherd ties the gate shut, sealing the suitors inside.

greek.greek: Τηλέμαχος κέλεταί σε, περίφρων Εὐρύκλεια,
greek.english: Eurycleia locks the women into their quarters at Telemachus's instruction.

herald.text: Scene 7. The Bow Sings. The beggar strings the bow with ease and shoots an arrow through all twelve axes; his son arms and joins him.

greek.greek: οἰκία τʼ ἐγγὺς ἐμεῖο τετυγμένα· καί μοι ἔπειτα
greek.english: Tells you that the stranger has not disgraced the house and signals the next phase.

theme.means: a sign, a token, a grave-marker: the scar and the bed are sēmata by which Odysseus is known

herald.text: Book 22. Slaughter in the Hall. The doors are locked, the weapons are gone, and the beggar holds the bow. Now Odysseus reveals himself and takes back his house by force. Scene 1. Antinous Falls. Odysseus throws off his rags, shoots the cruelest suitor, and announces who he is to the stunned, unarmed men.

greek.greek: τὸν δʼ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
greek.english: Odysseus strips off his rags, leaps onto the threshold, and pours the remaining arrows before him.

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Scene 2. Eurymachus Bargains and Attacks. A suitor leader offers to repay everything; Odysseus refuses and kills him, and his son spears another attacker.

greek.greek: σμερδαλέα ἰάχων· ὁ δʼ ἁμαρτῆ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
greek.english: Odysseus shoots Eurymachus in the chest.

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 3. The Storeroom Arms the Defenders. The son brings armor and spears for his father and the herdsmen, but leaves the storeroom door open.

greek.greek: ὣς φάτο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ φίλῳ ἐπεπείθετο πατρί,
greek.english: Telemachus runs to the storeroom and brings shields, helmets, and spears for Odysseus, Eumaeus, Philoetius,

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 4. Melanthius Arms the Suitors. The traitor goatherd sneaks weapons to the suitors through the open door; the herdsmen catch him and tie him up.

greek.greek: Ἀμφίνομος δʼ Ὀδυσῆος ἐείσατο κυδαλίμοιο
greek.english: Odysseus bind his hands and feet, hoist him by a rope to the rafters, and leave him suspended in pain.

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Scene 5. Athena Tests the Battle. The goddess, disguised as an old friend, turns aside the suitors' spears and fills them with terror.

greek.greek: εὗρεν ἔπειτʼ Ὀδυσῆα μετὰ κταμένοισι νέκυσσιν,
greek.english: Odysseus, I have not forgotten you.

theme.means: the singer, the bard: the poem's own maker inside the poem

herald.text: Scene 6. The Hall Is Cleared. The last suitors are killed; Odysseus spares the singer and the herald, whom his son says were forced to serve.

greek.greek: εὗρεν ἔπειτʼ Ὀδυσῆα μετὰ κταμένοισι νέκυσσιν,
greek.english: Spare me, Odysseus, and pity me.

theme.means: the homecoming. The Odyssey is the poem of one man's nostos; our word nostalgia is the ache for it

herald.text: Scene 7. The Disloyal Maids. The nurse names twelve maids who sided with the suitors; they clean the hall and are hanged, and the goatherd killed.

greek.greek: μή πω τήνδʼ ἐπέγειρε· σὺ δʼ ἐνθάδε εἰπὲ γυναιξὶν
greek.english: Identifies twelve maids who consorted with the suitors and mocked the household.

theme.means: reckless folly, the arrogance that brings its own ruin: the crews', the suitors'

herald.text: Scene 8. The House Calls Penelope. Odysseus purifies the hall with fire; loyal servants embrace him, and the nurse goes to wake the queen.

greek.greek: οἶσε θέειον, γρηΰ, κακῶν ἄκος, οἶσε δέ μοι πῦρ,
greek.english: Bring sulfur and fire so the hall can be purified.

theme.means: the wife, she who shares the bed

herald.text: Book 23. The Great Rooted Bed. The suitors are dead. Now the queen must decide whether this stranger is truly her husband after twenty years. Scene 1. Eurycleia Wakes Penelope. The old nurse tells the queen her husband is home and has killed the suitors; she cannot believe it.

greek.greek: εὗρον ἔπειτʼ Ὀδυσῆα μετὰ κταμένοισι νέκυσσιν
greek.english: Odysseus is home, here in this house, and every suitor lies dead in the hall.

theme.means: the fatherland, home ground

herald.text: Scene 2. Penelope Studies the Stranger. The queen sits facing the stranger in silence; their son scolds her, and Odysseus has the house prepare a cover story.

greek.greek: ἕζετʼ ἔπειτʼ Ὀδυσῆος ἐναντίη, ἐν πυρὸς αὐγῇ,
greek.english: She and Odysseus share private signs.

theme.means: cunning intelligence, the craft of the mind. Odysseus's own gift, and Athena's

herald.text: Scene 3. The False Wedding Noise. Music and dancing make neighbors think a wedding is happening, hiding the killings; the queen still holds back.

greek.greek: αὐτὰρ κὰκ κεφαλῆς κάλλος πολὺ χεῦεν Ἀθήνη
greek.english: Odysseus bathes while Athena restores his stature and beauty.

theme.means: glory, what is heard of a man: fame that outlives him in song

herald.text: Scene 4. The Bed Test. The queen orders their bed moved; he protests he built it around a living tree, their private secret, and she embraces him.

greek.greek: νύκτα μὲν ἐν περάτῃ δολιχὴν σχέθεν, Ἠῶ δʼ αὖτε
greek.english: Athena holds back dawn while husband and wife weep and reunite.

theme.means: the open sea

herald.text: Scene 5. Odysseus Tells the Remaining Journey. In bed, husband and wife tell each other their years apart; he admits one last journey still awaits him.

greek.greek: ἀρνειὸν ταῦρόν τε συῶν τʼ ἐπιβήτορα κάπρον,
greek.english: Travel inland with an oar and appease Poseidon.

theme.means: grey-eyed, bright-eyed: Athena's epithet

herald.text: Scene 6. Departure for Laertes. At dawn the king, his son, and the herdsmen arm themselves and slip out of town to reach his father's farm.

greek.greek: οὐ μέν τοι θυμὸς κεχαρήσεται· οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτὸς
greek.english: See nothing, say nothing, until I send for you.

theme.means: a trick, a snare: the horse, the bed, the web Penelope weaves and unweaves

herald.text: Book 24. Peace. The killing is over, but the dead men's families want blood. Odysseus goes to find his aged father before the town turns against him. Scene 1. The Suitors Enter Hades. The god who guides the dead leads the suitors' spirits to the underworld, where great warriors of the past wait.

greek.greek: ἠδὲ παρʼ Ἠελίοιο πύλας καὶ δῆμον ὀνείρων
words: one wing of a pair of double gates
greek.english: Hermes pass Ocean, the White Rock, the Gates of the Sun, and the land of dreams.

theme.means: a portion, one's share, fate

herald.text: Scene 2. Agamemnon Hears of Penelope's Fidelity. Among the dead, a suitor tells how Odysseus returned and killed them, and the spirits praise the queen's faithfulness.

greek.greek: πεζοί θʼ ἱππῆές τε· πολὺς δʼ ὀρυμαγδὸς ὀρώρει
words: one who fights from a chariot
greek.english: Agamemnon and Achilles debate the honor of their deaths and funerals.

theme.means: a god, a power, a fate: something divine at work you cannot name

herald.text: Scene 3. Odysseus Tests Laertes. Odysseus finds his grieving father working alone in an orchard, tests him with a lie, then cannot help revealing himself.

greek.greek: αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσῆϊ τόδε δὴ πέμπτον ἔτος ἐστίν,
greek.english: Odysseus claims to have hosted Odysseus years earlier and watches his father collapse in grief.

theme.means: a sign, a token, a grave-marker: the scar and the bed are sēmata by which Odysseus is known

herald.text: Scene 4. The Scar and the Orchard Trees. He proves himself with his scar and the trees his father gave him as a boy; the old man collapses in joy.

greek.greek: ὄγχνας μοι δῶκας τρισκαίδεκα καὶ δέκα μηλέας,
greek.english: Names the thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees, forty fig trees,

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live

herald.text: Scene 5. Laertes Is Restored. The father is bathed and made strong again, and the farm household feasts, while news of the killings spreads through town.

greek.greek: μήτηρ γρηῦς Σικελή, ἥ σφεας τρέφε καί ῥα γέροντα
greek.english: Dolius and his sons return from the fields, recognize Odysseus, and join the feast.

theme.means: a suitor, the men eating Odysseus's house away

herald.text: Scene 6. The Families Demand Revenge. In town, the suitors' families mourn; Eupithes ignores warnings and leads armed relatives toward the farm for revenge.

greek.greek: ὣς φάτο δάκρυ χέων, οἶκτος δʼ ἕλε πάντας Ἀχαιούς.
greek.english: Medon and Phemius testify that a god fought beside Odysseus.

theme.means: the singer, the bard: the poem's own maker inside the poem

herald.text: Scene 7. Zeus and Athena Set the Terms. The goddess asks the king of the gods whether to allow war or peace; Zeus decides Odysseus stays king and peace returns.

greek.greek: ὡς ἦ τοι κείνους Ὀδυσεὺς ἀποτίσεται ἐλθών;
greek.english: Let Odysseus be king over them all the days of his life.

theme.means: the homecoming. The Odyssey is the poem of one man's nostos; our word nostalgia is the ache for it

herald.text: Scene 8. The Last Clash. The relatives attack; the old father kills their leader with a spear, and the fighting threatens to become another slaughter.

greek.greek: κεῖνος μέν τοι ὅδʼ αὐτὸς ἐγώ, πάτερ, ὃν σὺ μεταλλᾷς,
greek.english: Son of Arceisius, dearest of all my friends, pray to the bright-eyed maiden and to Father Zeus.

theme.means: the wife, she who shares the bed

herald.text: Scene 9. Athena Makes Peace. The goddess commands both sides to stop, Zeus sends a thunderbolt, and she binds king and people in a lasting peace.

greek.greek: ἀλλʼ ὅτε δή μιν ἔγειρε Διὸς νοός αἰγιόχοιο,
greek.english: But that was the bolt of Zeus at your feet, and I will not argue with it.

theme.means: the spirit, the heart that surges: where anger, courage and longing live
